zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Secondary lexical reference: *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html License: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ The BnF scan remains the primary evidence; review corrections and chosen readings are distinguished in the line notes.

runs.text: Pato brauo que eſta ẽtre os caniços.

lines.note: Rogan is a wild duck living among reeds, marked as written usage by upright S. This headword confirms that the preceding page's bottom Rogan is a catchword, not extra body text.
This separate Rǒgan means an aged face, explicitly explained by Voitaru cauobaxe. The Portuguese velho is divided after ve-; it is not the duck-name definition above.
Completes the old-face gloss and supplies the written-register label S. The label is upright, unlike the Portuguese adjective fragment.

Rǒguet denotes the last month of the Japanese year, equated with Xiuaſu. The second pass resolves the small vowel mark as a caron, unlike the circumflex of the following hazy-moon entry; the gloss reads mes, not the OCR mer.
Completes the description of the final month of the Japanese year. Iapão is Portuguese typography, not a Japanese term for whole-word toggling.
This homophonous entry concerns a hazy moon among clouds. The Japanese reads Voborozzuqi, with r and doubled z, and the Portuguese reads Lũa dantre nuuens rather than the garbled OCR sequence.
Completes the hazy-moon definition: it is only faintly visible. The clause explains the obscuration by clouds in the previous row.
Rǒguet is a bright moon, paraphrased by Fogaracana tçuqi. The visible caron distinguishes it from the immediately preceding hazy-moon entry, which has a circumflex.
Adds resplendent to the preceding bright-moon gloss. The whole word is a physical continuation and is kept on its own row.

Rôgui names the creatures Qera and ari; the Portuguese identifies the former by name and continues with ant below. The conspicuous gap in embedded Q era is retained rather than silently closing the supplied reading.
Completes the pair with ant, translating ari. This short row belongs to the preceding creature-name entry.
Roguio is the fish described in Japanese as Suzuqino vuo. The Portuguese merely says a fish so called; no additional species identification is imposed.
Roguiǔ combines donkey and ox, explicitly listed as Roba and vxi. The initial o is unmarked, unlike the old-cattle entry below.
Rǒguiǔ means an old cow or ox. The final character is the marked vowel ǔ, not OCR f; the Latin alternative vel remains part of the printed gloss.
Rǒgo refers to the period after becoming old, as Voite nochi explains. The separate words de ſer are restored from the OCR's fused form.
The example concerns a good or satisfying life in old age. The abbreviated Portuguese cõ- continues as contentamento on the next physical line.
Completes contentamento and specifies satisfaction after growing old. The second pass confirms that depois is printed continuously here, removing the provisional OCR space within the word.

runs.text: Ceſto de vimes, ou canaſtra. Vt,

lines.note: Rôgu is a wicker basket or hamper. The example begins Ito-, which joins the next row's no rôgu rather than standing as an independent headword.
Completes Ito-no rôgu, a basket associated with silk. The Portuguese Ceſto de ſeda is copied without deciding whether it describes the contents or construction.

runs.text: Pao em que ſemete, & joga o remo.

lines.note: Rogvi denotes the wooden fitting in which the oar is inserted and worked. The scan has a v-shaped type in the headword, retained as Rogvi rather than regularizing the u/v spelling; the Japanese reading remains rogui.

runs.text: Caminho eſtreito, & eſcuſo que vai pera

lines.note: Rogi is a narrow, secluded path. The Portuguese destination clause continues below; the ornamental R is upright, not a separately italicized initial.

runs.text: a caſa do Chanoyu, &c. Itẽ, Caminho dentro da

lines.note: The first path leads to the tea-ceremony house; the second lies within a temple enclosure. Chanoyu is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation, and dentro corrects the OCR's extra i.

runs.text: cerca dalgũa varela por onde ſe vai à cella dal-

lines.note: Continues the temple-enclosure sense, describing access to a monk's cell. The abbreviated dalgũa and divided dal- are retained as printed.

runs.text: gum bonzo, ou a outra caſa que eſta dentro.

lines.note: Completes the path's destination as a monk's cell or another house inside the enclosure. The Portuguese bonzo belongs to the gloss, not to a Japanese quotation.
Rǒgio means an old woman, directly paraphrased by Voitaru vonna. The entire headword is upright despite the OCR's isolated italic R.
Rǒgiǔ denotes elders or senior leaders, paraphrased by Toxiyorixu. Anciãos corrects OCR Auciãos; the Portuguese principais continues on the next row.

runs.text: pais cabeças como os do cõſelho dalgum ſenhor:

lines.note: Completes principais and identifies the elders as leading council members of a lord. The abbreviated cõſelho and terminal colon are preserved.

runs.text: & tãbem ſe toma por hum ſoo como hum dãtre

lines.note: Explains that the term can also designate one individual from among the elders. The print reads tãbem and the abbreviated dãtre, not OCR lãbem and dãire.
Completes the explanation of an individual selected from these old and senior men. This is still the scope note for Rǒgiǔ.
Rǒjeqi is discourtesy, disorder, or injury, with Quantai as the Japanese equivalent. The doubled initial RR is an OCR artifact; the scan contains one ordinary R and a single long ſ in Deſcorteſia.
Completes desordem and adds injury. The example Saijǒno rǒjeqi intensifies the misconduct; the abbreviated Portuguese Grã- continues as Grande.
Completes the example as great discourtesy or disorder, then begins the phrase Rǒjeqi-uo ſuru. The scan has t in deſcorteſia, not OCR i.
Completes Rǒjeqi-uo ſuru: to commit an injury or disorder. The Japanese object particle continues across the physical line break.

runs.text: O que faz injuria, ou agrauo.

lines.note: Rǒjeqinin is a person who commits an injury or offense. The Portuguese phrase faz injuria is legible as two words, unlike the fused OCR reading.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de ceſto, ou canaſtrinha.

lines.note: Rôji denotes a kind of basket or small hamper. The headword has a circumflex over o in the scan, rather than the draft's caron.
Roji is equated with Sagui and glossed as a heron. The unmarked o distinguishes the printed form from the basket entry above.
Rǒjin means an old person, paraphrased by Voita fito. A paragraph sign begins the example about an old person leaning on a staff; both headword and example are upright.
Completes the example as relying on a staff. The Portuguese bordão confirms the walking-stick sense of tçuye, and the terminal punctuation is retained.
Rôjǒ concerns remaining enclosed or besieged in a fortress, as Xironi comoru explains. The two long-o marks have different directions in the printed form.
Completes the fortress definition and supplies the verbal example Rôjǒſuru. Vt is italic apparatus; the Japanese expression is upright and printed without an internal space.
Rôju is an old tree, directly equated with Voiqi. The source's circumflex is retained rather than harmonized with other old-age compounds.

Rǒjǔ is equated with Rǒdô and glossed as household servants of a lord. The final letter of apparent dalgi is narrow and dotted in the scan; that anomalous reading is retained rather than silently expanding the expected abbreviation dalgũ. The worn impression remains a nonblocking caveat.
Rǒmai denotes a provision or supply of rice for a journey. The grave in arròz is visible and is kept in the historical Portuguese form.
Romei is a brief life, figuratively explained as the life of dew by Tçuyuno inochi. The headword is upright throughout.
Rǒmô concerns senility or decrepitude, explained by Voi foruru. The Portuguese describes a person impaired by old age and continues with an abstract-noun alternative below.

runs.text: que cedura: ou idade decrepita. Vt,

lines.note: Continues the decrepitude gloss, retaining the unusual printed spacing que cedura and its colon. The example begins Rǒ and continues with mô below. At the right edge only a short dot-like mark is visible; a period is chosen provisionally instead of supplying a full hyphen from the word division.

Completes the example begun as Rǒ on the preceding row: becoming senile or decrepit. The opening mô is a continuation, not a new headword; the preceding dot-like mark is preserved without normalizing the divided form.
Rômon is a gate with a structure above it, paraphrased by Yagurano cado. The scan restores initial R and the final l of Portuguese qual.
Completes the architectural description with an upper floor or platform over the gate. The Portuguese alternatives remain at the source's level of detail.
Rǒ muxa means an old soldier. The printed space within the Japanese expression is retained, even though many adjacent compounds are closed up.
Ron denotes dispute or contention; Ronuo ſuru supplies the verbal example. The scan reads Diſputa, correcting the OCR's o for p.

runs.text: ¶ Item groſa, ou tratado ſobre algũ texto, ou

lines.note: Introduces a second Ron sense: a gloss or treatise on a text or subject. Groſa is retained as the printed word, not normalized or doubled.
Completes the treatise definition with materia, subject matter. The following physical row is Rondan; the provisional pi. between them is not an independent printed line.
Rondan is debate, paraphrased by Ronji danzuru. This complete row is retained under its original ID; the overlapping OCR-only c2-l007 is removed without losing text.
Rǒnen is old age, literally explained by Voita toxi. The Portuguese gives the concise equivalent velhice.

runs.text: Nome de hum liuro da China que tra-

lines.note: Rongo is the name of a Chinese book. The Portuguese starts a clause explaining its subject matter; tra- continues as trata rather than the OCR's tru-.
Completes trata de couſas moraes, stating that the book concerns moral matters. The physical division of trata is preserved.

Rongui concerns debate or reasoning. The Japanese Ronzuru is restored from OCR Honzuru; the apparent cotcuari is retained provisionally rather than silently imposing expected cotouari, because the c/o impression is worn.
Ronhacu contrasts old and young people, as Voitari and vacaxi explain. The initial o appears unmarked in this copy; the lexical index's long-vowel form does not by itself justify adding a mark.
Completes the old-and-young pair with young men. It translates vacaxi and remains a separate physical continuation.
Rǒni is an aged nun, paraphrased by Voitaru ama. The Portuguese describes a shaven-headed woman like a nun; ama corrects the malformed OCR amra.
Completes the Portuguese comparison with a nun. This row finishes the same Rǒni definition.
The principal forms of Ronji describe disputing or arguing. The Portuguese altercar has t, not the OCR's second l; the abbreviated Japanese forms are not expanded in the transcription.
The example means debating right and wrong. Initial I in Iefi is a historical consonantal spelling; the Portuguese comparison continues below.

runs.text: bom, ou mao, razão, ou contra razão.

lines.note: Completes the debate's alternatives as good or bad, right or contrary to reason. The historical mao is retained without modernization.
Rǒnin is glossed as an exile or banished person. The definition is preserved without replacing it with a narrower modern samurai-related explanation.
Ronnin is a disputant, literally a person who argues. Its initial R and doubled n distinguish it from the preceding Rǒnin; the OCR's B is corrected.

runs.text: traz demanda ſobre algũa couſa cõ outro.

lines.note: Completes the disputant's description as someone pursuing a suit or claim against another. Both Portuguese abbreviation tildes are retained.
Rǒnô denotes an aged farmer, paraphrased by Voita tatçucuri. The Portuguese Laurador and ja are separate words in the scan.
Ronſo concerns disputing and bringing a complaint. The Portuguese continues as a coordinated definition below; the terminal mark is a comma, not the OCR's period.
Adds accusing to the preceding definition of legal or argumentative action. The long ſ in acuſar is preserved.

runs.text: Certo chapeo que trazião as mo-

lines.note: Roppǒgaſa is a kind of hat formerly worn by women. The scan supports doubled p and a continuous headword, correcting the OCR Ropi ǒgaſa; the Portuguese mulheres is divided after mo-.
Completes the historical statement that women wore this hat in earlier times. The source's antiguamente spelling is not modernized.

runs.text: Solda, ou miſtura de outro metal que fi-

lines.note: Rǒqe denotes solder or an admixture of another metal. The Portuguese relative clause continues with fica on the next row; metal and que are separate words.

runs.text: ca em algũas peças douro, ou prata deſmãcha-

lines.note: Describes solder left on dismantled gold or silver pieces. The abbreviated deſmãcha- is preserved across the line break rather than expanded to modern spelling.

runs.text: das, ou tiradas de ſeu lugar. ¶

lines.note: Completes dismantled or removed from their place, then begins an example. The scan reads tiradas rather than tiradar and includes the full Japanese subject phrase Rǒqega, including its final a.
Completes Rǒqega aru: these pieces have this solder on them. The opening aru is part of the Japanese example begun above.
This Rǒqen denotes an old dog, directly paraphrased by Voita inu. It is a separate entry from the robust-old-age sense on the next row.
This Rǒqen describes a vigorous old person, as Toxiyori ſucuyacana explains. The Portuguese valente continues on the following row; no hyphen is supplied where the worn edge does not establish one.
Completes valente and gives the alternative explanation old age with strength. This is the robust-old-age sense, not the old-dog entry.
Roqen concerns becoming manifest or revealing something. Both the headword and verbal example begin with R, correcting the OCR's B.
The example says that something is already manifest. The Japanese reads cotogia, not cotugia; the Portuguese manifeſ- has f before the long ſ and continues below.

Completes manifesta and adds public. At the far right, the parenthesized ſair de caſa is displaced continuation text for Rôqio on the next physical row; its position is preserved explicitly rather than joining it to publica or moving it below.

Rôqio means remaining secluded, as Comori iru explains. Its Portuguese definition ends with ſem and continues in the displaced phrase ſair de caſa on the preceding physical row: remaining inside without going out.
Roqua is the flower of reeds, explicitly explained by Axino fana. The closing S. is an upright written-register label.
Rǒquai concerns an old person's cares or thoughts, paraphrased by Voino vomoi. The scan supports vomoi rather than the OCR vemoi; the Portuguese pensamentos is divided after pen-.
Completes pensamentos de velho, the thoughts of an old person. The long ſ is retained at the start of this continuation.

Rǒrai means reaching old age. The apparent printed Vei is retained provisionally rather than silently replacing it with expected Voi; the worn e/o deserves later human inspection. Velhice and the terminal comma are restored from the scan.
Adds becoming old as an equivalent explanation. This completes the preceding Rǒrai entry.
The principal forms of Rorimeqi describe being restless or agitated. The scan contains a final conjunction &, which the OCR omitted.

runs.text: deſaſoſegado, ou com medos, ſobreſalto, ou com

lines.note: Expands the restless state to unease, fear, or alarm. The historical spelling deſaſoſegado is retained without modernizing its consonants.

runs.text: algum outro aluoroço como de hoſpedes, &c.

lines.note: Adds other kinds of commotion, such as the bustle caused by guests. This explains a broader sense than fear alone.
Rorirori is the corresponding adverbial expression for restless behavior. The scan restores andar from the OCR aidar; Aduer. is italic grammatical apparatus.
Completes the adverbial gloss as agitation with fear and similar states. The visible historical aluoraçado is retained rather than normalized to alvoroçado, and medo replaces the garbled OCR nedo.
The catchword anticipates Rǒrô at the opening of f425. Its last vowel has a circumflex; no separate full stop is visible before the right rule. The word is retained at the far right in roman type.
